summary: Defines how MPLS label switching can run over Frame Relay networks, including the model and generic mechanisms used. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3034 explains how to run MPLS label switching on Frame Relay equipment. The label goes into the field that normally holds the circuit identifier, so the switch can swap labels the way it already swaps circuits. The rest of the label stack uses the ordinary MPLS header, and because Frame Relay switches cannot count hops, the memo makes the ends of a segment adjust the packet's time-to-live instead of every switch in between.

subtitle: How a Frame Relay switch can act as an MPLS label switching router by carrying labels in the DLCI field.

tldr.problem: Frame Relay switches are built to swap a circuit identifier, and they cannot count hops the way IP routers count TTLs. That makes them a poor fit for MPLS, which needs a label that can be swapped and a TTL that can be tracked.
tldr.mechanism: The memo makes the DLCI field of the Frame Relay header carry the top MPLS label, so a Frame Relay switch becomes a label switching router with no change to the frame format. Everything else in the label stack travels in the generic MPLS shim header, and the missing hop counting is handled by propagating the length of a segment so the ingress or egress can decrement the TTL once for the whole segment.
tldr.outcome: The result is that Frame Relay networks can carry MPLS label switched paths, and can mix with switches that use other encapsulations on the same path. The price is a set of Frame Relay specific LDP messages, a restriction on when several virtual circuits may be merged, and the fact that the label distribution protocol itself has no protection against misdirected or forged labels.

facts.label: Default hop count
facts.value: 1 when LDP gives none or an unknown value

facts.label: Default virtual circuit parameters
facts.value: Zero committed information rate, so the DE bit is set but no frames are dropped

facts.label: TTL decrement
facts.value: 0, 1, or the number of hops of the LSP segment

today: RFC 3034 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It is a companion to RFC 3032 on the MPLS label stack encoding and to RFC 3035 on label switching with ATM, and it builds on the MPLS architecture of RFC 3031 and the Label Distribution Protocol of RFC 3036.

sections.title: Running MPLS on Frame Relay Switches
sections.content:
RFC 3034 defines the model and the generic mechanisms for Multiprotocol Label Switching on Frame Relay networks. It extends and clarifies parts of the MPLS architecture of RFC 3031 and the Label Distribution Protocol of RFC 3036 as they apply to Frame Relay, and it is a companion document to the MPLS label stack encoding of RFC 3032 and to the label switching over ATM specification of RFC 3035.

It is possible to use Frame Relay switches as label switching routers. Such switches run network layer routing algorithms such as OSPF or IS-IS, and their forwarding is based on the results of those algorithms, so no specific Frame Relay routing is needed.

When a Frame Relay switch is used for label switching, the top, current, label on which the forwarding decision is based is carried in the DLCI field of the Frame Relay data link layer header of the frame. The other information that travels with the top label, but is not processed by Frame Relay switching, together with any further labels if the packet is multiply labelled, is carried in the generic MPLS encapsulation.

Frame Relay permanent virtual circuits can be configured to carry label switching traffic. The DLCIs are then used as MPLS labels, the Frame Relay switches become Frame Relay label switching routers, the MPLS traffic is encapsulated according to this specification, and it is forwarded on the basis of network layer routing information.

The requirement keywords in the memo are to be interpreted as defined in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says a Frame Relay switch can be a label switching router. The switch still runs ordinary IP routing, but the label it forwards on is the circuit identifier it already uses, and the other label fields ride in a standard MPLS header inside the frame.

sections.title: The Terms the Memo Adds
sections.content:
The memo defines the vocabulary it uses, on top of the terms of the MPLS architecture.

An LSR is a label switching router: a device that implements the label switching control and forwarding components of the architecture. A LC-FR interface is a label switching controlled Frame Relay interface, a Frame Relay interface controlled by the label switching control component, where packets traversing it carry labels in the DLCI field. An FR-LSR is an LSR with one or more LC-FR interfaces that forwards frames between two such interfaces using the labels carried in the DLCI field. An FR-LSR domain is a set of FR-LSRs mutually interconnected by LC-FR interfaces, and the Edge Set of such a domain is the set of LSRs connected to the domain by LC-FR interfaces.

The encapsulation terms describe what a packet is wearing at a given moment. The forwarding encapsulation is the type of MPLS encapsulation, Frame Relay, ATM or Generic, of a packet that determines its MPLS forwarding, or the network layer encapsulation if the packet is forwarded on its IP header. The input encapsulation is the type of encapsulation a packet has when it is received on an LSR interface, and the output encapsulation the type it has when it is transmitted on one. The input TTL is the MPLS TTL of the top of the stack when a labelled packet is received, or the IP TTL if the packet is not labelled, and the output TTL the same value when the packet is transmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo names the pieces: a Frame Relay interface under label switching control, a switch that forwards labels between such interfaces, the set of those switches, and the switches at the edge of the set. It also names the three encapsulation types a packet can have as it enters, is forwarded on, and leaves a switch.

sections.title: What Frame Relay Switches Can and Cannot Do
sections.content:
The MPLS architecture allows considerable freedom in how an LSR is built, but an FR-LSR is constrained by the capabilities of the hardware it already has and by the restrictions on frame format imposed by Multiprotocol Interconnect over Frame Relay and by the Frame Relay standards. Some special procedures are needed to work within those constraints, and four characteristics matter most.

First, the label swapping function is performed on fields in the frame's Frame Relay data link header, which dictates the size and placement of the labels in a packet. The size of the DLCI field can be 10 bits, which is the default, or 23 bits, and it can span two or four bytes of the header.

Second, there is generally no capability to perform a TTL decrement, as is done on IP headers in routers.

Third, congestion control is performed by each node based on parameters passed at circuit creation, and flags in the frame headers may be set as a consequence of congestion or of exceeding the contractual parameters of the circuit.

Fourth, although in a standard switch it may be possible to configure multiple input DLCIs to one output DLCI, giving a multipoint-to-point circuit, multipoint-to-multipoint virtual circuits are generally not fully supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Frame Relay hardware limits what an MPLS switch can do. The label lives in a field of 10 or 23 bits, the switch cannot count down a TTL, congestion is handled per circuit, and virtual circuits between many endpoints are not really supported.

sections.title: Label Encapsulation
sections.content:
By default all labelled packets should be transmitted with the generic label encapsulation of RFC 3032, using the frame relay null encapsulation mechanism. The null encapsulation puts a Q.922 address of two or four octets, holding the DLCI, in front of the MPLS packet. The length of the Q.922 address, called n in the memo, can be 2 or 4 octets.

The Q.922 representation of a DLCI is given in canonical order, the first bit stored in the least significant, that is right-most, bit of a byte in memory. In the 10 bit form the first octet holds the high order part of the DLCI with two zero bits after it, and the second octet holds the low order part with three zero bits and a final one bit. In the 23 bit form the first octet again holds the high order part of the DLCI with two zero bits, the second octet holds 14 more bits of DLCI with four zero bits, the third octet holds eight more bits of DLCI with a zero bit, and the fourth octet holds the low order bits of the DLCI with a zero bit and a one bit.

The use of the frame relay null encapsulation means that labels implicitly encode the network protocol type. The rules for constructing the label stack and the error messages returned to the frame source are in RFC 3032.

The generic encapsulation contains n labels for a label stack of depth n, where the top stack entry carries significant values for the EXP, S and TTL fields but not for the label, which is instead carried in the DLCI field of the Frame Relay data link header encoded in Q.922 address format.
sections.plainLanguage: Labelled packets are sent with the standard MPLS header, but the label itself is left out of it and put in the Frame Relay circuit identifier field instead. The identifier is written in the bit order the Q.922 standard defines, in either a 10 bit or a 23 bit form.

sections.title: Frame Relay Label Switching Processing
sections.content:
Label switching works by associating labels with routes and using the label value to forward packets, including to determine the value of any replacement label. In an FR-LSR the top, current, MPLS label is carried in the DLCI field, and it implicitly carries information about the network protocol type. For two connected FR-LSRs a full-duplex connection must be available for LDP, and the DLCI for that LDP virtual circuit is assigned by configuration, much like the DLCI used to run IP routing protocols between switches. Apart from that configured value, the DLCI values used for MPLS in the two directions of a link may be treated as belonging to two independent spaces, so virtual circuits may be half-duplex with their own DLCI in each direction. The allowable ranges of DLCIs, the size of the DLCIs and support for virtual circuit merging must be communicated through LDP messages, and the range of DLCIs used for labels depends on the size of the DLCI field.

An LSP is homogeneous when the LSRs on it use the same encoding of the label stack on every hop, and heterogeneous when they do not. The MPLS architecture supports LSPs with different label stack encodings on different hops, and a labelled packet received by an LSR must be decoded to find the current label stack, operated on to find the new label value, and encoded again before transmission. A network may mix Frame Relay switches with other LSRs that use the Generic MPLS shim header or ATM encapsulation, and an LSR with both Frame Relay and Generic MPLS interfaces may swap off a Frame Relay encoded label and replace it with a label in a Generic MPLS header.

FR-LSRs should operate on loop free FR-LSPs or LSP Frame Relay segments. They should use loop detection and may use loop prevention mechanisms as described in the MPLS architecture and in LDP. The MPLS TTL in the label stack is the mechanism used to suppress loops and to limit the scope of a packet. A packet should emerge from a path with the same TTL it would have had if it had traversed the same routers without label switching, and if it travels along a hierarchy of LSPs the total number of LSR hops traversed should be reflected in the TTL when it emerges.

The initial value of the MPLS TTL is loaded into a newly pushed label stack entry from the previous TTL value, whether that came from the network layer header when no previous label stack existed or from a pre-existing lower level label stack entry. A FR-LSR switching same level labelled packets does not decrement the MPLS TTL, and a sequence of such FR-LSRs is a non-TTL segment. When a packet emerges from a non-TTL LSP segment, the TTL should reflect the number of LSR hops it traversed. In the unicast case this is achieved by propagating a meaningful LSP length or LSP Frame Relay segment length to the ingress nodes, so that the ingress decrements the TTL before forwarding packets into the segment. In the multicast case the meaningful length is propagated to the egress node, which decrements the TTL before forwarding packets out of the segment.

When an ingress FR-LSR determines that, after decrementing, a packet's TTL will expire before the packet reaches the egress of the non-TTL segment, it must not label switch the packet. Instead it treats it as an expired packet and returns an ICMP message to its source, or it forwards the packet as an unlabelled packet with a TTL that reflects IP forwarding. If the incoming TTL is 1, only the first option applies.

The calculation that turns the input TTL into the output TTL depends on the input, forwarding and output encapsulations, and is written as the output TTL equals the input TTL minus D of the three encapsulations, or in brief the output TTL equals the input TTL minus d, where d has three possible values: 0, 1, or the number of hops of the LSP segment. For unicast, d is 0 when all three encapsulations are Frame Relay; d is 1 when the forwarding encapsulation is Generic MPLS and the output encapsulation is Generic MPLS; and d is the number of hops of the LSP segment when the forwarding encapsulation is Generic MPLS or the network layer and the output encapsulation is Frame Relay. For multicast, d is 0 when all three are Frame Relay; d is 1 when the forwarding encapsulation is Generic MPLS or the network layer and the output encapsulation is Frame Relay; and d is the number of hops of the LSP segment when the input encapsulation is Frame Relay, the forwarding encapsulation is Generic MPLS or the network layer, and the output encapsulation is anything.

The number of hops of the LSP segment is the hop count attached to the label used when the packet is forwarded, if LDP provided one when it distributed the label, that is, if the LDP message carried a hop count object. If LDP did not provide a hop count, or provided an unknown value, the default is 1. When a label binding is sent upstream, the hop count of the binding from downstream must be incremented by 1 and the result passed upstream, while the unknown value is passed unchanged. If the new hop count exceeds the maximum value, the FR-LSR must not pass the binding upstream but must send an error upstream.

Label processing differs by position in the path. When a packet first enters an MPLS domain it is forwarded by normal network layer forwarding, except that the outgoing encapsulation includes an MPLS label stack with at least one entry. The frame relay null encapsulation carries information about the network layer protocol implicitly in the label, which must be associated only with that network protocol, and the TTL field of the top label stack entry is filled with the network layer TTL that resulted from network layer forwarding. For unicast packets the MPLS TTL should be decremented by the number of hops of the Frame Relay LSP or segment, and for multicast packets by 1. The encapsulated packet is then passed to the Frame Relay data link driver with the top label as the output DLCI and forwarded onto the virtual circuit to the next LSR.

In a core FR-LSR the current label is carried in the DLCI field, and just as in conventional Frame Relay the DLCI of an arriving frame is looked up in the DLCI Information Base, replaced with the corresponding output DLCI, and transmitted on the outgoing interface. In the top level label stack entry, all fields except the label information are of current significance.

At the end of a Frame Relay LSP the FR-LSR pops the label stack. If the popped label is the last one, the network layer protocol being carried must be inferred from the value of that label, because the label stack carries no explicit information about it. If it is not the last label, the previous top level MPLS TTL is propagated to the new top label stack entry. If the FR-LSR is the egress switch of a Frame Relay segment of a hybrid LSP and the end of the segment is not the end of the LSP, the packet is forwarded onto the next segment on the basis of the Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry, the output label is set from that entry, and the MPLS TTL is decremented by the appropriate value for the type of output interface and transmit operation. For unicast packets the MPLS TTL should be decremented by one if the output interface is generic, or by the number of hops of the next ATM segment if the output interface is an ATM, non-TTL, interface. For multicast packets it should be decremented by the number of hops of the Frame Relay segment being exited.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching works as in any MPLS network: the label is looked up and replaced. The difference is that Frame Relay switches do not count down the TTL, so the length of a run of Frame Relay switches is worked out in advance and the ingress or egress subtracts it in one go. If the TTL would run out inside the run, the packet is not switched and an error is sent back instead.

sections.title: The Label Switching Control Component
sections.content:
To support label switching, a Frame Relay switch must implement the control component of label switching, which consists primarily of label allocation and maintenance procedures. Label binding information may be communicated by several mechanisms, one of which is the Label Distribution Protocol.

Because the label switching control component uses information learned directly from network layer routing protocols, the switch must participate as a peer in those protocols, such as OSPF or IS-IS. In some cases LSRs may use other protocols, such as RSVP, PIM or BGP, to distribute label bindings, and in those cases a Frame Relay LSR should participate in them too.

Where Frame Relay circuits are established through LDP or RSVP or others with no involvement from traditional Frame Relay mechanisms, the circuit establishing contractual information, such as input and output maximum frame size, incoming and outgoing requested and agreed throughput, incoming and outgoing acceptable throughput, incoming and outgoing burst size, incoming and outgoing frame rate used in transmitting, and congestion control, may be passed to the FR-LSRs through RSVP or can be statically configured. Congestion control and frame header flagging as a consequence of congestion are then done by the FR-LSRs in a similar fashion to traditional Frame Relay circuits. With the goal of emulating a best-effort router by default, the default virtual circuit parameters, in the absence of LDP, RSVP or other mechanisms setting such parameters, should be zero committed information rate, so that input policing sets the discard eligibility bit in incoming frames but no frames are dropped. Control and state information for the circuits based on MPLS may be communicated through LDP.

Supporting label switching on a Frame Relay switch requires conformance only to the Frame Relay Forum implementation agreement for framing, bit-stuffing, headers and FCS, and not to section 2.3 of it, which covers PVC control signalling procedures, also known as the LMI. Q.933 signalling for PVCs and SVCs is not required. PVC and SVC signalling may be used for non-MPLS, standard Frame Relay, PVCs and SVCs when both are running on the same interface as MPLS.

The memo also allows hybrid switches. The existence of the label switching control component on a Frame Relay switch does not stop the switch supporting the Frame Relay control component defined by the ITU and the Frame Relay Forum on the same switch and the same interfaces; the two control components operate independently. How such a device operates is beyond the scope of the memo, but only a small amount of information has to be consistent between the two control components, such as the portions of the DLCI space available to each.
sections.plainLanguage: A Frame Relay switch that does label switching has to run IP routing as a peer, and it may take its circuit settings from a label distribution protocol or from configuration. It does not have to implement the Frame Relay PVC signalling at all. A switch may also keep running ordinary Frame Relay control on the same ports at the same time, with the two systems working side by side.

sections.title: Label Allocation and Maintenance
sections.content:
The downstream-on-demand label allocation and maintenance mechanism must be used by FR-LSRs that do not support virtual circuit merging, and may also be used by those that do. It applies to hop-by-hop routed traffic.

At the edge of an FR-LSR domain, an edge LSR that selects a FR-LSR as the next hop for a route sends it an LDP request message for a label binding. When the downstream LSR answers with an LDP mapping message, the label is stored in the Label Information Base as an outgoing label for that route. The mapping message may carry a hop count object, which is the number of hops a packet will take to cross the FR-LSR domain to the egress FR-LSR when using this label, and that value may be stored for TTL calculation. The edge LSR can then use MPLS forwarding for that traffic.

When a member of the edge set receives an LDP request from a FR-LSR, it is the egress FR-LSR for that route. It allocates a label, creates a new entry in its Label Information Base, places the label in the incoming label component of the entry, and returns a mapping message with the allocated label to the peer that made the request. That mapping carries the hop count object with the value 1.

When a routing calculation makes an edge LSR change its next hop, and the former next hop was inside the FR-LSR domain, the edge LSR should notify the former next hop with an LDP release message that the label binding is no longer needed.

An FR-LSR that receives a request from a peer over an LC-FR interface allocates a label, creates a new entry in its Label Information Base with the label in the incoming label component, and propagates the request downstream. In ordered control mode it waits for the downstream mapping before returning its own mapping upstream, and in that case it increments the hop count it received from downstream and uses that value in the mapping it returns. In independent control mode it returns the binding upstream without waiting, using a reserved value for the hop count that means unknown; the correct value is sent later. The memo leaves the choice between the two as an implementation or configuration decision.

A FR-LSR may receive several binding requests for the same route from the same peer. It must generate a new mapping for each request and retain any existing mappings, and it should also generate a new binding request toward the next hop for each request it receives.

When a label binding is no longer needed, the LSR may deallocate the label and destroy the binding, which is the conservative label retention mode, and if it does so it should notify the next hop that the binding is no longer needed. In liberal label retention mode the binding is kept and may be reused only if a request arrives for the same route with the same hop count as the request that originally created it.

When a route changes, label bindings are re-established from the point where the route diverges from the previous route, and LSRs upstream of that point are, with one exception, unaffected. Whenever an LSR changes its next hop for a route and the new next hop is an FR-LSR reachable over an LC-FR interface, it should request a binding from the new next hop for each matching entry in its Label Information Base.

When an FR-LSR receives a binding from a downstream neighbour it may already have given a corresponding binding upstream, either because it uses independent control or because the new binding is the result of a routing change. It then extracts the hop count from the new binding and increments it by one, and if the new hop count differs from the value previously given upstream, including the case where the upstream neighbour was given the value unknown, it must notify that neighbour of the change. Each FR-LSR in turn increments the hop count and passes it upstream until it reaches the ingress edge LSR.

If a request that an FR-LSR originated downstream is not satisfied, the FR-LSR should destroy the binding it created in response to the received request and notify the requester with an LDP withdraw message. When an LSR determines that it has lost its LDP session with another LSR, it must discard any binding information learned through that connection, and may destroy the bindings that were created as a result of requests from that peer.

Merging FR-LSRs. The discussion so far assumes that an edge LSR requests one label for each prefix in its routing table that has a next hop in the FR-LSR domain. In fact one label can be requested for several routes, and many-to-one mappings between routes and labels, using the notion of forwarding equivalence classes, conserve the number of labels. Conserving label space may be restricted where the frame traffic requires Frame Relay fragmentation, because Frame Relay fragments must be transmitted in sequence and fragments of distinct frames must not be interleaved. If the fragmenting FR-LSR ensures that all the fragments of a frame are sent in sequence without interleaving with fragments of other frames, label conservation can be performed.

With label conservation, a FR-LSR that already has an outgoing label binding for a route does not need to issue a downstream request when it gets an upstream request; it may allocate an incoming label and return that instead, and packets arriving with it are forwarded after replacing the label with the existing outgoing label. If the FR-LSR has an outstanding request for an outgoing binding it need not issue another. It must respond with a new binding for every upstream request, but it may need to send only one binding request downstream. If a routing change makes the FR-LSR select a new next hop for one of its routes it may release the binding for that route from the former next hop, and if it does not already have a corresponding binding for the new next hop it must request one. If a new binding is obtained with a hop count that differs from the old one, the FR-LSR increments it by one if it is not unknown and notifies the upstream neighbours that have bindings for that route. To ensure that loops are detected, if the new hop count exceeds the maximum value the label values for that route must be withdrawn from all the upstream neighbours to whom a binding was previously sent.

LDP messages specific to Frame Relay. LDP messages exchanged between two Frame Relay LDP peers may carry three Frame Relay specific items. The Frame Relay Label Range has reserved bits, a Len field giving the number of bits of the DLCI, where the value 0 means 10 bits and the value 2 means 23 bits while 1 and 3 are reserved for future use, and a Minimum DLCI and a Maximum DLCI, each a 23 bit field giving the lower and upper bound of a block of DLCIs supported by the originating FR-LSR, right justified in the field. The Frame Relay Merge item has a one bit Merge field, where 0 means merge is not supported and 1 means it is. A FR-LSR that supports virtual circuit merging must ensure that fragmented frames from distinct incoming DLCIs are not interleaved on the outgoing DLCI. The Frame Relay Label item has reserved bits, a Len field with the same values as before, and the DLCI field holding the binary value of the label, whose significant 10 or 23 bits are encoded into the DLCI field of the Frame Relay data link header.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is asked for on demand: the edge router asks the next switch for a label, and the switch asks its own next hop, and so on. The number of hops to the far end is counted as the request travels and passed back to the edge, which uses it to set the TTL. Several routes can share one label to save label space, as long as fragmented frames are not interleaved.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo looks at two areas: frame traffic and label distribution.

MPLS encapsulation has no effect on authenticated or encrypted network layer packets, so an IP packet that is authenticated or encrypted incurs no change. The MPLS protocol has no mechanisms of its own to protect against misdirection of packets or the impersonation of an LSR, whether by accident or by malicious intent. Altering, by accident or by forgery, an existing label in the DLCI field of the Frame Relay data link layer header, or one or more fields in a potentially following label stack, affects the forwarding of that frame.

The label distribution mechanism can be secured by applying the appropriate level of security to the underlying protocol that carries the label information, whether authentication or encryption, as described for LDP.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS itself does nothing to protect a label. Someone who can change the label in a frame can change where the frame goes, and MPLS has no way of telling a real switch from an impostor. The way to protect it is to secure the protocol that distributes the labels.

items.title: DLCI field size
items.text: 10 bits by default, or 23 bits, spanning two or four bytes of the header.

items.title: No TTL decrement
items.text: There is generally no capability to decrement a TTL, as a router does on an IP header.

items.title: Congestion control
items.text: Each node does its own, from parameters passed at circuit creation, and sets frame header flags as a result.

items.title: No multipoint to multipoint
items.text: Several input DLCIs can map to one output, but virtual circuits between many endpoints are generally not supported.
